Facebook Twitter Print Email ‘This is not about politics. This is about people’: UN warns of impact of deadly drone strikes in Sudan 3 November 2026 Humanitarian Aid Intensifying drone attacks on civilian infrastructure across Sudan are disrupting electricity, water and fuel supplies, putting lives at risk and hampering the delivery of humanitarian aid, the UN’s top official in the country has warned. Hundreds of aid trucks are stranded due to fuel shortages, while hospitals are struggling to maintain lifesaving services, including dialysis. Speaking to UN News , UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator Denise Brown urged the international community to intervene to end the fighting and provide urgently needed funding, saying: “This is not about politics. This is about people.” UN News: Let me begin by asking about the escalating drone attacks and their devastating impact on civilians. What are you seeing on the ground? Denise Brown: There's been an intense pattern of drone strikes over the past couple of weeks. What we're seeing is what appear to be targeted attacks on civilian infrastructure, which, of course, is protected under international humanitarian law . Sources of energy and fuel appear to be systematically targeted and destroyed. So already there's an apparent violation here. Essential services are also being massively disrupted. Colleagues from the World Health Organization ( WHO ) were at a hospital just outside Khartoum, and the electricity went out because of these drone strikes. The hospital has no generator, no solar panels. So, the 25 people who need dialysis had their treatment stopped, point blank . There was nothing they could do without electricity. This affects women giving birth, children and everyone else. The same goes for water. There are also widespread fuel shortages . In Khartoum, there are queues kilometres long as people wait for fuel. But what we're seeing is tuk-tuk drivers – those who take people to work and to the market. These are people who earn a daily wage and are having to wait several days in a row to get fuel, which means they're not earning an income. That's the direct impact of the widespread intensification of drone strikes and their immediate consequences for the civilian population. We've also seen markets and displacement sites being hit. So, the attacks are widespread and, I have to say, increasingly worrying for us and scarring for the population. © UNICEF/Mohammed Jamal A displaced mother walks through a refugee camp in Tawila, North Darfur, after fleeing the siege of Al Fasher. UN News: Amid this escalation, can you tell us more about the UN's response on the ground and its main priorities right now? Denise Brown: The UN humanitarian community works alongside international and national non-governmental organizations and local communities. It's the communities who are always the first to respond and who are consistently on the front line. But we have one priority, which is to save lives . Because of the severe rainfall deficits over the past couple of months, we now have a new dimension to what is already a pre-existing catastrophe, quite frankly. Farmers have been faced with a lack of rainfall, so we know that in some parts of Darfur and Kordofan, people are on the move looking for food. But that's just an additional layer; it's not the only factor we're dealing with. We have millions of people displaced who continue to be displaced because of the war. Basic social services have been disrupted, and the health system, despite best efforts, has been decimated . Severe acute malnutrition, as we know from the UN Children Fund ( UNICEF )’s studies, is very high, exceeding the emergency threshold in many parts of the country, particularly those directly affected by the war. Our priority is to work with partners to provide services and supplies to people who, very frankly speaking, would die without that assistance. UN News: What are your greatest concerns at this point? Denise Brown: The UN has a very big supply chain for food, nutritious products, shelter and non-food items. That's really one of the added values of the UN humanitarian response. But we have hundreds of trucks stuck because of a lack of fuel . Sometimes we face bureaucratic impediments, which we work with the authorities to overcome, and there's been huge progress regarding our visas and permits.
